background.definition: Contact dermatitis is classified as either irritant (ICD) or allergic (ACD), and results in skin irritation following exposure to chemicals. Irritant contact dermatitis occurs following direct contact with the offending substance, whereas ACD is a delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction requiring prior sensitization.

list.listitem: In 2005, the US Bureau of Labor Statistics showed an annual incidence rate of 44 cases of occupational skin diseases per 100,000 workers, of which contact dermatitis makes up the large majority.

In 2004, an estimated 72 million Americans had been diagnosed at some point in their lives with contact dermatitis, and more recent data suggests 41 to 77% of US children suffer from allergic contact dermatitis (ACD).
Based on data from the National Health Interview Survey (n = 30,074), occupational contact dermatitis had a prevalence of 1700 per 100,000 workers for the year 1988.
A cross-sectional study (n = 1501) involving patch testing of Denmark students age 12 to 16 years revealed a point prevalence of 15.2% for contact allergy.

A systematic review and meta-analysis showed a 20.1% pooled prevalence of ACD, and a prevalence of 16.5% in those less than 18 years old. Women had a significantly high prevalence (27.9%) as compared to men (13.2%). Nickel was the most commen allergen (11.4%), follwed by fragrance mix (3.5%) and cobalt (2.7%).
In 1984, occupational skin diseases, including contact dermatitis, resulted in an estimated indirect cost of $11 million lost productivity/year.
Direct and indirect costs were estimated to be in excess of $22 million.
$1.35 billion was spent on treating contact dermatitis, including physician visits and medications.
Allergic contact dermatitis (ACD) was the third most common reason for outpatient dermatology visits in 2004.
Occupational skin diseases, including contact dermatitis, are the most commonly reported nontrauma-related occupational illnesses.
Chemical exposure.
Plants: poison ivy, oak, and sumac, which contain the oil urushiol the most common cause of allergic reactions in the United States, tomatoes.
Metals: nickel most common internationally, and gold, cobalt, chromate.

Topical medications and preservatives: most commonly neomycin, bacitracin, as well as steroids, anesthestics (lidocaine), antifungals, thimerosal, methylchloroisothiazolinone/methylisothiazolinone (MCI/MI) commonly found in cosmetics and other products, parabens and formaldehyde, and para-phenylenediamine commonly found in henna tattoos and hair dyes, liquid skin adhesive used to close surgical wounds.
Rubber chemicals: latex, carbamates, mercaptobenzothiazole, thiuram, black rubber mix.
Fragrances: Balsam of Peru, aromatherapy including lavender, peppermint, tea tree oil, linalool and limonene and ylang-ylang.
Occupational irritants: solvents, oils, lubricants, fuels, soaps, cleansers, detergents, "face mask dermatitis"
Most common in children: nickel sulfate, ammonium persulfate, gold sodium thiosulfate, thimerosal, and toluene-2,5-diamine (p-toluenediamine).
Methylisothiazolinone has been causing very high rates of allergy in Europe and USA recently and may have peaked.

Hydroxyethyl methacrylate (HEMA) has been recommended to add to the British Society for Cutaneous Allergy baseline series for screening increasing rates of acrylate allergy with nail and cosmetic product.
Irritant contact dermatitis (ICD) is caused by skin injury, direct cytotoxic effects, and cutaneous inflammation from contact with specific irritants. Symptoms usually occur immediately.

Allergic contact dermatitis (ACD) is caused by a type IV, T-cell-mediated delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction. Sensitization occurs when skin is first exposed to an offending chemical. The absorbed chemical modifies the appearance of keratinocytes, resulting in recognition by Langerhans cells. Langerhans cells carry the chemical to lymph nodes where CD4 T cells trigger cytokine release, resulting in a clonal population of memory T cells. These memory T cells then return to the site of initial exposure and produce more inflammation. Microscopic changes show spongiotic vesicle formation around adnexal ducts. Symptoms generally take several hours to occur.
After-work creams, moisturizers with high lipid content, cotton glove liners, fabric softeners, and possibly barrier creams prevent ICD. B
Rhus dermatitis can be prevented by topical skin protectants and bentoquatam/bentonite clay–based barrier formulas (I.C. Ivy Block). B
Avoid known allergens; occupational irritant contact dermatitis (ICD) can be prevented with industry-specific organizational hazard controls. C
British Academy of Dermatologists guidelines recommend skin care and skin protection creams to prevent occupational contact dermatitis. C
A thorough history and physical, focusing on exposure history and dermatitis pattern, is crucial for making the diagnosis of contact dermatitis. C
Patch testing is the gold standard for making the diagnosis of contact dermatitis, although not all patients require testing. B
Differentiating atopic dermatitis from contact dermatitis, especially on the hands and face, may be challenging, hence patch testing should be considered. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Lesions have more scale and follow a typical distribution for atopic dermatitis (flexor areas and the face in children).
Lesions are more scaly, round, and eczematous; margins are more distinct.
Lesions are commonly confined to the scalp and face.
Groups of vesicles form that are painful and ulcerate.
Lesions are more widespread bullous or vesicular.
Distribution is consistent with sun-exposed areas only.
Lesions are more scaly and lichenified.
More redness, possible wound drainage or fluid collection, pain

list.listitem: History should assess for possible exposures to known allergens and irritants, as well as symptom progression, location, and timing of the symptoms in relation to possible exposure. A thorough social history should be obtained addressing possible work- or hobby-related exposures. Pruritus is usually present.
Physical exam should include a thorough skin exam, paying particular attention to potential areas of contact with offending agents.

Lesions with sharp borders and angles are virtually pathognomonic for ACD. ACD typically presents with an erythematous, scaling, papulovesicular dermatitis at the site of contact, often with a linear distribution pattern and indistinct margins.
Contact dermatitis can also present with bullae acutely, and oozing may be seen. Chronic irritation can cause scaling, fissuring, and lichenified dermatitis.
In allergic contact dermatitis (ACD), previously sensitized patients generally experience symptoms 12 to 48 hours after re-exposure, and the disease may last 1 to 3 weeks.
Rhus dermatitis causes symptoms within 4 to 96 hours after exposure, symptoms peak within 1 to 14 days, and new lesions can present up to 21 days after exposure.
Patch testing is the gold standard for diagnosing ACD, with a sensitivity and specificity of approximately 70%, though sensitization rates are significantly higher in appropriate referrals.

British Academy of Dermatology guidelines recommend offering patch test with a baseline series of allergens to all patients with possible contact dermatitis, with additional allergens added based on symptoms and history. If the results are unexpectedly negative at day 4, re-read at day 7.

The most commonly used patch test is the Thin-layer Rapid Use Epicutaneous (TRUE) test, which consists of 28 common allergens and 1 negative control. Given that over 3700 allergens have been identified as causing ACD, it has been suggested that the TRUE test may be missing clinically important allergens.
Testing based upon geographic location and patient history can increase the TRUE test's sensitivity.
In patients with a clear exposure history, and physical findings consistent with contact dermatitis, diagnosis can confidently be made without confirmatory testing.
When the diagnosis of allergic contact dermatitis is questionable, or symptoms are chronic, patch testing should be performed.
Patch testing is also helpful to differentiate between ACD and ICD, with a negative patch test suggesting ICD.
The first goal of treatment is identification of the offending agent and discontinuation of exposure when possible. C
For initial therapy and when symptoms persist despite allergen removal and irritant removal, moderate- to high-potency steroid preparations are recommended, as is topical tacrolimus. A
Lipid-rich moisturizers may effectively treat irritant contact dermatitis (ICD). B

Topical moderate- to high-potency steroid preparations are often effective in the treatment of both allergic and irritant contact dermatitis and are recommended as first-line drug therapy. Tacrolimus 0.1% ointment is also effective, well tolerated, and shows results similar to topical corticosteroids therapy. These treatments are not a substitute for removal of the offending or potentially offending allergen or for skin protection.
Second line therapies include phototherapy and immunomodulators administered systemically such as methotrexate and mycophenolate mofetil.
Lipid-rich moisturizers may effectively treat ICD. Antihistamines may relieve pruritus.

Oral steroids may be useful for severe or widespread disease (>20%). The recommended dose is 0.5 to 1 mg/kg daily for 5 to 7 days, with a maximum starting dose of 60 mg daily. The rate of steroid taper depends on the severity and duration of the disease, and ability to avoid the causative irritant. A typical tapering regimen takes 2 to 3 weeks.
Level B evidence suggests off-label use of azathioprine can be effective for parthenium dermatitis (an airborne plant allergen contact dermatitis).

For chronic hand dermatitis, British Association of Dermatology guidelines recommend psoralen plus UVA (PUVA), cyclosporine, and alitretinoin; however, relevant studies do not specifically evaluate patients with contact dermatitis.
Current studies are investigating the use of topical Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors for chronic hand dermatitis, especially as it overlaps with chronic hand eczema, and early reports seem promising.
Targeted biologics may be helpful to treat recalcitrant contact dermatitis.
After exposure, the allergen should be cleaned from the skin as soon as possible.
Cool, wet compresses of water or Burow's solution, lukewarm baths, and oatmeal baths can help ease symptoms of pruritus.
Wet-to-dry dressings may be considered if oozing is present.
When exposed to irritant plants, patients should be educated to wash contacted clothing as soon as possible to eliminate spread via oil contact.

Barriers and emollients or barrier creams may prevent dermatitis in industrial settings. Moisturizers used alone or in combination with barrier creams may result in clinically important protective effect either in the long-term or short-term for the prevention of occupational irritant hand dermatitis. Barrier creams alone may have slightly protective effect but not clinically important with limited evidence from 1533 patients data in this Cochrane review.
Probiotics lack evidence of efficacy for eczema, but have not yet been studied for contact dermatitis.
Educational interventions as an adjunct to conventional treatment may lead to improvements in disease severity and quality of life, but quality of evidence is low.
Given the natural history of rhus dermatitis, and the potential for rebound dermatitis if treatment duration is too short, generally 2 to 3 weeks of oral steroid treatment is recommended.

Antibiotics may be required if bacterial superinfection is observed. Cephalexin 500 mg twice daily and topical retapamulin 1% twice daily are equally effective in treating secondarily infected dermatitis.

As much as 75% of patients with occupational contact dermatitis may have intermittent or persistent symptoms over a 10-year period. Despite changing occupation, 40% of patients may remain symptomatic. C
For mild contact dermatitis, prognosis is likely determined by the adequacy of removing the trigger and preventing re-exposure. C
Avoidance can prevent contact dermatitis.
Most irritant contact dermatitis is on the hands so gloves can offer protection, depending on the nature of the chemicals involved.
It may be possible to substitute a nonirritating agent for the causative agent.
Barrier creams are of questionable value but after-work creams may be useful.
Those with persistent eczematous eruptions should undergo patch testing.
Healthcare workers with dermatitis have an increased risk of bacterial colonization, and alcohol gel is less damaging to skin than antiseptics or soap.
In the geriatric population, skin dryness or xerosis may increase the incidence of irritant dermatitis.
Maternal use of topical corticosteroids has not been associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes.
Topical corticosteroid use has not been associated with adverse effects among lactating mothers and infants. However, when possible, the nipple and areola should be avoided.

Because of the limited amount of skin surface available for testing, and the potential risk of active sensitization, children under 6 years-old should only be tested if there is a high degree of suspicion for ACD, and only with the specific allergens suspected.
Children have an increased incidence of positive patch testing because of better delayed hypersensitivity reactions.
